french.tip: 'Être' (to be): je suis, tu es, il est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils sont.
Passé composé: auxiliary 'avoir' + past participle. Most verbs use 'avoir'. The participle normally doesn't agree.
'Aller' is irregular: je vais, tu vas, il va, nous allons, vous allez, ils vont.
Weather in the past uses imparfait: il pleuvait, il faisait beau.
'Faire' = to do/make. Irregular: je fais, il fait, nous faisons, ils font. Used in many fixed expressions.
Three question forms: intonation ('Tu viens?'), 'est-ce que', or inversion ('Viens-tu?').
'Au' = à+le, 'aux' = à+les. Mandatory contractions. 'À la' and 'à l'' don't contract.
Ouvrir to ouvert: shared pattern with couvrir, découvrir, offrir.
Être is the only verb with an irregular imparfait stem: et-.

german.tip: 'sich' is a reflexive pronoun — many German verbs require it even when English doesn't (e.g., 'sich erinnern' = 'to remember').
In German present tense, the verb always takes second position in statements — this is the V2 rule.
Relative clauses use der/die/das as relative pronouns — they match the noun's gender but take the case from their role in the relative clause.
This uses 'sein' as the Perfekt auxiliary — verbs of movement or change of state take 'sein' instead of 'haben'.
'Sollen' (should/supposed to) expresses obligation or advice: 'Du sollst mehr Wasser trinken'.
German imperative: du-form drops -st (Komm!), ihr-form keeps -t (Kommt!), Sie-form keeps Sie after verb (Kommen Sie!).
'Möchte' (would like) is the polite way to express wants: 'Ich möchte einen Kaffee' — preferred over 'will'.
Formal imperative keeps 'Sie' after the verb: 'Kommen Sie!' The 'wir' form means 'let's': 'Gehen wir!'
Separable prefixes (zurück, hin, her, weg, raus, um, ab, zu, zusammen) always split off in main clauses and land at the sentence end.
'Dass' (that) sends the conjugated verb to the end of its clause: 'Ich weiß, dass er morgen kommt'.
Regular verbs in German present tense follow a predictable pattern: stem + -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en.
'Ein/eine' changes form by gender and case: ein (masc/neut nom), eine (fem nom), einen (masc acc).
'Der' marks masculine nouns in nominative case. Every German noun has a fixed gender you must memorize.
'Die' is used for feminine singular and all plural nouns in nominative/accusative case.
Dative changes 'ein/mein/sein' to 'einem/meinem/seinem' (masc/neut) and 'einer/meiner/seiner' (fem).
German has three genders (der/die/das) — there are patterns, but many must simply be memorized with each noun.
Frequency words like 'immer' (always), 'oft' (often), 'jeden Tag' (every day) signal habitual present tense.
'Sein' (to be) is fully irregular: ich bin, du bist, er ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie sind.
'Das' marks neuter nouns. Nouns ending in -chen or -lein are always neuter (diminutives).
'Zu' + dative expresses direction toward a person or place: 'zum Arzt' (to the doctor), 'zur Schule' (to school).
'Bis' can be a preposition (until) or conjunction (until). As a conjunction, the verb goes to the end of its clause.
The prefix at the end signals a separable verb — in main clauses, the prefix splits off and goes to the sentence end.
'Bei' + dative means 'at/near/at the home of': 'bei meinen Eltern' (at my parents' place), 'beim Essen' (during the meal).
Comparative adjectives still take regular endings when before a noun: 'ein schnelleres Auto' (a faster car).
'Als' connects comparatives: 'größer als' (bigger than). Don't confuse with 'wie' which means 'as...as' in equality.
Irregular comparisons to memorize: gut→besser→am besten, viel→mehr→am meisten, gern→lieber→am liebsten.
Monosyllabic adjectives often gain an umlaut in comparative/superlative: alt→älter→am ältesten, jung→jünger→am jüngsten.
German passive uses 'werden' + past participle: 'Das Buch wird gelesen' (is being read), 'wurde gelesen' (was read).
'Den' is accusative masculine — only masculine articles change in accusative: der becomes den, ein becomes einen.
Dative signals the recipient or beneficiary of an action: 'Ich gebe dem Mann das Buch' — the man receives the book.
'Nach' + dative means 'after' or 'toward': 'nach dem Essen' (after the meal), 'nach Deutschland' (to Germany).
Reflexive pronouns match the subject: mich/mir (I), dich/dir (you), sich (he/she/it/they), uns (we), euch (you pl.).
Comparative adverbs work the same way: 'schneller laufen' (run faster), 'lauter sprechen' (speak louder).
'Ob' (whether) creates indirect yes/no questions with verb-final order: 'Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt'.
'Je...desto/umso' creates proportional comparisons: 'Je mehr, desto besser' (The more, the better).
Superlatives have two forms: 'am schönsten' (predicative) and 'der/die/das schönste' (attributive, before a noun).
Some adjectives with -d, -t, -s, -z add -e- before -sten: 'am kürzesten' (shortest), 'am wildesten' (wildest).
Double comparatives don't exist in German: 'more better' = just 'besser'. The -er suffix already handles it.
Coordinating conjunctions (und, aber, oder, denn) keep normal word order; subordinating ones (weil, dass, wenn) send the verb to the end.
'Immer + comparative' expresses 'more and more': 'immer schneller' (faster and faster), 'immer besser' (better and better).
'aus' (from/out of) always governs the dative case — no exceptions.
'bei' (at/near) always governs the dative case — no exceptions.
'nach' (after/to) always governs the dative case — no exceptions.
'auf' (on) + dative = location. Accusative would indicate direction/movement toward.
'seit' (since/for) always governs the dative case — no exceptions.
'für' (for) always takes accusative — no exceptions.
'mit' (with) always governs the dative case — no exceptions.
'Dass' (that) introduces a noun clause — verb goes to the end. Often replaceable by dropping 'dass' and using V2 order.
'durch' (through) always takes accusative — no exceptions.
'Nicht' placement follows strict rules — typically before what it negates, and always before the final verb element (participle/infinitive/prefix).
The V2 rule: in German main clauses, the conjugated verb is always the second element, regardless of what comes first.
'Ein-' is a separable prefix meaning 'in/into' (einkaufen, einladen, einsteigen) — it splits to the end.
'Auf-' as a separable prefix often means 'up' or 'open' (aufstehen, aufmachen) — it goes to the sentence end.
'von' (from/of) always governs the dative case — no exceptions.
Movement and state-change verbs use 'sein': 'Ich bin gegangen' (went), 'Er ist gestorben' (died), 'Sie ist eingeschlafen' (fell asleep).
'Seit' + dative marks duration from a starting point: 'seit einem Jahr' (for/since a year) — always dative, never accusative.
Regular past participles: ge- + stem + -t: 'gemacht' (made), 'gekauft' (bought). Irregular ones change the vowel: 'gesungen' (sung).
Perfekt = haben/sein + past participle: 'Ich habe gegessen' (I ate/have eaten). This is what you'll hear in everyday conversation.
Two-way prepositions (an, auf, in, etc.) take dative for location (wo?) and accusative for direction (wohin?).
'War/waren' (was/were) — Präteritum of 'sein', preferred over Perfekt even in spoken German.
After 'mit' (with), always use dative: 'mit dem Auto' (by car), 'mit meiner Freundin' (with my girlfriend).
Daily routines often use reflexive verbs: 'sich anziehen' (get dressed), 'sich duschen' (shower), 'sich setzen' (sit down).
Reciprocal meaning with plural subjects: 'Sie lieben sich' can mean 'they love themselves' or 'they love each other'.
'Sich' is used for all 3rd person and formal 'Sie': 'Er freut sich', 'Sie freuen sich', 'Sie freuen sich' (formal).
Reflexive verbs in perfect tense use 'haben': 'Ich habe mich gefreut' (I was happy), never 'bin' with reflexives.
English speakers often forget the reflexive — 'I remember' = 'Ich erinnere mich', not just 'Ich erinnere'.
Accusative vs. dative reflexive: 'Ich wasche mich' (I wash myself) vs. 'Ich wasche mir die Hände' (I wash my hands).
'Sich' with prepositions creates common phrases: 'sich auf etwas freuen' (look forward to), 'sich für etwas interessieren' (be interested in).
Some verbs are only reflexive: 'sich beeilen' (hurry), 'sich weigern' (refuse), 'sich schämen' (be ashamed).
Word order: reflexive pronoun comes right after the conjugated verb in main clauses: 'Ich erinnere mich an...'
Extended adjective constructions pack complex modifiers before the noun — a hallmark of formal written German.
'Ich bin' means 'I am' — 'sein' (to be) is irregular: ich bin, du bist, er/sie ist.
'in' (in) + accusative = direction/movement. Dative would indicate static location.
Prefix 'mit' at the end — the separable verb splits in main clauses, with the prefix jumping to the sentence end.
Verbs ending in -ieren skip ge-: 'studiert' (studied), 'telefoniert' (phoned) — these are usually loan words.
In northern Germany, Präteritum is more common in speech. In southern Germany and Austria, Perfekt dominates for everything.
'Sein', 'haben', and modals (können, müssen, etc.) use Präteritum even in speech: 'Ich war' not 'Ich bin gewesen'.
Dative changes articles: der→dem, die→der, das→dem, die(pl)→den(+n). Mastering these transforms is essential.
Reflexive pronouns match the subject: ich→mich/mir, du→dich/dir, er/sie/es→sich. Accusative or dative depends on the verb.
In practice, most adjective endings are -e or -en — the system looks complex but the two endings cover 90% of cases.
Without any article, the adjective carries the full case/gender signal: 'kaltes Wasser' (cold water), 'guter Wein' (good wine).
Plural adjectives after definite articles always end in -en: 'die großen Häuser', 'den großen Häusern', 'der großen Häuser'.
After indefinite articles (ein/eine), the adjective takes over the article's job of showing gender: 'ein großer Mann' vs. 'eine große Frau'.
The accusative masculine is the key exception: 'den großen Mann', 'einen großen Mann' — the -en ending signals accusative masculine.
After definite articles (der/die/das), adjective endings are mostly -e or -en: 'der große Mann', 'dem großen Mann'.
'Wenn' (if/when) sends the verb to the clause end — the main clause then starts with the verb (inversion).
Formal German avoids contractions: 'an dem' instead of 'am', 'in dem' instead of 'im' — though this is mostly in very formal writing.
Business German uses set phrases: 'Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren' (Dear Sir/Madam), 'Mit freundlichen Grüßen' (Kind regards).
The 'Sie' form (formal you) governs verb conjugation and pronoun choice — switching from 'du' to 'Sie' changes the entire sentence.
Prefix 'an' at the end — the separable verb splits in main clauses, with the prefix jumping to the sentence end.
Adjective 'neue' — its ending depends on the article type, case, and noun gender. After definite articles, usually -e or -en.
'um' (around/at) always takes accusative — no exceptions.
Double infinitive in Perfekt with modals: 'Ich habe kommen können' (I was able to come) — the modal stays as infinitive.
Certain verbs always take dative objects: 'helfen' (help), 'danken' (thank), 'gefallen' (please), 'gehören' (belong to).
Written narratives use Präteritum: 'Er ging nach Hause' (He went home) — but the same speaker would say 'Er ist nach Hause gegangen'.
Verbs like gefallen, gehören, schmecken, fehlen, helfen, passen always take a dative object: 'Das gefällt mir'.
German imperative has three forms: du (Komm!), ihr (Kommt!), Sie (Kommen Sie!) — the verb comes first in all forms.
Adjectives derived from city names end in -er and never change: 'der Berliner Zoo', 'die Münchner Küche' — no declension.
Color adjectives follow the same rules: 'das rote Auto' (definite), 'ein rotes Auto' (indefinite), 'rotes Licht' (no article).
All subordinating conjunctions (dass, weil, wenn, ob, als, obwohl, während, bevor, nachdem) push the verb to the clause end.
Multiple adjectives before a noun all take the same ending: 'ein großes, altes, rotes Haus' — they agree with each other.
Relative pronouns must match the gender/number of the noun they refer to: 'die Frau, die...' (feminine), 'das Kind, das...' (neuter).
Predicate adjectives (after sein/werden) never take endings: 'Das Haus ist groß' — only attributive adjectives (before nouns) do.
Konjunktiv II uses 'würde + infinitive' for most verbs, but sein (wäre), haben (hätte), and modals use their own forms directly.
German freely combines nouns into compounds — the last word determines gender and meaning: 'Haustür' (house door) is feminine because 'Tür' is.
Perfect tense creates a bracket: 'Ich habe (content) gegessen' — the past participle closes the verbal bracket at the end.
In main clauses, the finite (conjugated) verb is always second, and non-finite verbs (infinitives, participles) go to the end.
Written German separates main and subordinate clauses with commas — formal style depends heavily on correct comma placement.
Three-verb chains in subordinate clauses: 'dass ich hätte kommen können' — all three verbs stack at the end.
Future tense also forms a bracket: 'Ich werde morgen nach Berlin fahren' — 'fahren' finishes the sentence.
With modal verbs, the main verb waits at the end as infinitive: 'Ich kann heute nicht kommen' — 'kommen' is at the end.
Register switching is crucial in German — using 'du' with a stranger or 'Sie' with close friends both create awkwardness.
Formal German avoids anglicisms: 'Besprechung' instead of 'Meeting', 'Rückmeldung' instead of 'Feedback' — especially in official texts.
German academic style uses longer paragraphs and fewer short sentences than English — directness is valued differently.
Academic German strings noun phrases together: 'Wirtschaftswachstumsförderungsgesetz' — compound nouns are a hallmark of formal style.
Hedging phrases signal academic caution: 'Es scheint, dass...' (It seems that...), 'Man könnte argumentieren' (One could argue).
Participle constructions replace relative clauses in formal writing: 'die betroffenen Personen' vs. 'die Personen, die betroffen sind'.
Nominalization converts verbs to nouns: 'Die Durchführung der Untersuchung' (The carrying out of the investigation) — dense but standard.
Compound nouns create precision: 'Forschungsergebnis' (research result), 'Handlungsbedarf' (need for action) — one word, clear meaning.
Impersonal 'es' constructions dominate: 'Es ist festzustellen' (It is to be noted), 'Es ergibt sich' (It results/follows).
Extended adjective constructions pack information before the noun: 'die in der letzten Woche durchgeführte Studie' (the study conducted last week).
Adjective 'neuen' — its ending depends on the article type, case, and noun gender. After definite articles, usually -e or -en.
Yes/no question — verb takes V1 position. German doesn't need a 'do' auxiliary.
'das' (nom./acc. neut.) introduces a relative clause — its case depends on its role within that clause.
German sentence structures follow strict verb-placement rules
German adjectives take endings only when placed before a noun — after 'sein' (is), they remain in base form.
'Aus-' is a common separable prefix (ausgehen, ausmachen, ausschalten) — it splits off in main clauses.
'Während' (while/whereas) — dual meaning: temporal (simultaneous) or contrastive (whereas). Context determines which.
'die' (nom./acc. fem./pl.) introduces a relative clause — its case depends on its role within that clause.
Präteritum is the written/narrative past tense. In speech, only sein (war), haben (hatte), and modals regularly use it.
Modal verbs take position 2 and push the main verb to infinitive at the end: 'Ich kann/muss/will/soll/darf ... [infinitive]'.
Du-imperatives of strong verbs with a→ä do NOT use the umlaut: 'Fahr!' (Drive!), 'Lauf!' (Run!) — not 'Fähr!' or 'Läuf!'
'Wenn' clauses put the verb at the end. If the wenn-clause starts the sentence, the main clause begins with the verb.
The genitive is thriving in written German even as it fades from casual speech — knowing it marks you as educated.
'Bevor' (before) — subordinating conjunction with verb-final. Both clauses usually share the same tense.
'der' (nom. masc.) introduces a relative clause — its case depends on its role within that clause.
Genitive masculine/neuter nouns add -s or -es: 'des Vaters' (of the father), 'des Kindes' (of the child).
In spoken German, relative clauses often simplify: 'Der Typ, wo ich gestern getroffen hab' — using 'wo' instead of the correct pronoun.
The case of the relative pronoun depends on its role in the relative clause: 'Der Mann, den ich sehe' — 'den' is accusative (object).
Unlike English, German never omits the relative pronoun: 'The man I saw' must be 'Der Mann, den ich sah' — 'den' is required.
'Wo' can replace preposition + relative pronoun for places: 'Die Stadt, wo ich wohne' — more common in speech.
Relative clauses are always set off by commas in German — this is not optional like in English restrictive clauses.
'Was' as a relative pronoun refers to entire clauses or indefinite things: 'alles, was ich weiß' (everything that I know).
Multiple relative clauses can nest: 'Das Buch, das der Mann, der hier war, gelesen hat' — the verbs stack at the end of each clause.
Prepositions come before the relative pronoun: 'Die Stadt, in der ich wohne' (The city in which I live) — never strand the preposition.
The passive voice shifts focus from the doer to the action. Use 'von + dative' for the agent: 'von dem Lehrer korrigiert'.
Konjunktiv I can express wishes in set phrases: 'Gott sei Dank' (Thank God), 'Es lebe die Freiheit' (Long live freedom).
Subordinate clauses push ALL verbs to the end: 'weil ich das Buch gestern gelesen habe' — finite verb comes last.
The verbal bracket (Satzklammer) is fundamental: the conjugated verb opens it in position 2, the rest closes it at the end.
The verbal bracket explains why Germans 'wait for the verb' — the key information often comes at the very end of the sentence.
In yes/no questions, the verb moves to first position but non-finite verbs still go to the end: 'Hast du das Buch gelesen?'
Academic German requires mastery of connectors: 'dennoch' (nevertheless), 'infolgedessen' (as a result), 'nichtsdestotrotz' (nonetheless).

dutch.tip: Dutch verb stems: remove -en, apply spelling rules (double vowels in closed syllables, devoice z→s, v→f).
'Ik ben' (I am) uses 'zijn' — the most irregular Dutch verb.
In Dutch, 'ik' always takes the bare verb stem — no -t or -en ending.
'Hebben' (to have) drops its -t ending with 'ik': 'ik heb', not 'ik hebt'.
Dutch present tense: remove -en from the infinitive for the stem, then add endings.
'Zijn' (to be) is fully irregular: 'ik ben', 'jij bent', 'hij is', 'wij zijn'.
"Er" has multiple uses: existential, locative, and prepositional.
'Mijn' (my) is a possessive pronoun — it doesn't change for de/het words.
Plural subjects (wij/zij/ze) always take the infinitive form: 'wij werken', 'zij lopen'.
Regular -en verbs: 'werken' → stem 'werk' + endings. 'Wij werken' keeps the infinitive form.
'Zijn' (to be) is the most irregular Dutch verb: ben/bent/is/zijn/was/waren/geweest.
Dutch uses V2 word order in main clauses.
The verb goes to the end in subordinate clauses: "...omdat ik werk" (because I work).
'Hoe' (how) forms questions about manner or degree: 'Hoe gaat het?'
Some adjectives double the final consonant: 'groot' -> 'grote', 'dik' -> 'dikke'.
Dutch adjective rule: add -e before nouns, EXCEPT with 'een' + het-word: 'een mooi huis' vs 'het mooie huis'.
In subordinate clauses, the verb moves to the end.
Dutch prepositions are tricky — 'in/op/aan/bij' all translate to 'at' in different contexts.
'Tot' (until): 'tot morgen' (until tomorrow), 'tot ziens' (see you).
Dutch temporal conjunctions (toen, terwijl, voordat) push the verb to the end of their clause.
'Enerzijds...anderzijds' (on one hand...on the other), 'niet alleen...maar ook' (not only...but also) are paired connectors.

swedish.tip: Swedish present tense is simple: one form for all persons. Just add -r to the verb stem.
Swedish word order: the verb always comes second in main clauses, regardless of what starts the sentence.
Swedish object pronouns: 'mig' (me), 'dig' (you), 'honom' (him), 'henne' (her), 'oss' (us), 'dem' (them).
This is a group 1 (-ar) verb — regular and predictable. Past tense adds -ade: 'tittar' → 'tittade'.
Swedish verbs don't change with person: 'jag talar', 'du talar', 'han talar' — same form for everyone.
This is a group 1 (-ar) verb — the largest and most regular verb group in Swedish.
Swedish present tense is formed by adding -r to the infinitive stem. It stays the same for all persons.
Swedish present tense: regular verbs simply add -r. The form is the same for all subjects.
Swedish uses compound words extensively — long words are usually separate words joined together.
Swedish word order: the verb is always in second position in declarative main clauses (V2 rule).
'Bo' → 'bor' (live): Group 3 verb — short infinitive, add -r for present.
If you're unsure of a verb's group, the infinitive ending helps: -a with present -ar = group 1; -a with present -er = group 2.
Swedish present tense adds "-r" to the infinitive: "talar" (speak/speaks).
'Gå' → 'går' (go/walk): Group 3 short verb — just add -r to the infinitive.
The V2 rule doesn't apply in subordinate clauses (after att, som, när, etc.) — there the subject comes before the verb.
Swedish verbs don't change with person: "jag talar", "du talar", "han talar".
Swedish present tense: add -r to the infinitive stem. Same form for all persons: jag/du/han/vi all use '-r'.
Swedish past tense has 4 verb groups with different endings: -ade, -de, -dde, irregular.
Swedish has two genders: "en" (common) and "ett" (neuter).
'Hur' (how) — for manner/degree: 'Hur mår du?' (How are you?), 'Hur långt?' (How far?).
Starting a sentence with a non-subject element creates an inversion: the verb stays second and the subject follows it directly.
Notice how the verb stays in second position even when time or place comes first. This V2 pattern is automatic for native speakers.
Swedish V2 order feels natural once you internalize it: the verb is the anchor at position two, everything else arranges around it.
"En" words: en bok (a book), boken (the book). "Ett" words: ett hus (a house), huset (the house).
In Swedish main clauses, the verb is always in second position — even when the sentence starts with a time expression or adverb.
Swedish keeps the verb second in statements. Starting with an adverb or object forces the subject behind the verb.
The V2 rule means if you start with something other than the subject, the subject must follow the verb: 'Igår köpte jag...' not 'Igår jag köpte...'
Definite form adjectives add "-a": "den stora bilen" (the big car).
When you front an adverb or object for emphasis, the verb must stay second — the subject simply moves to accommodate it.
V2 word order is one of Swedish's core rules — it applies to every declarative main clause, regardless of what comes first.
Unlike English, Swedish requires the verb in position two. When emphasis shifts the first element, the subject slides to third position.
In main clauses, sentence adverbs (inte, alltid, aldrig, redan) come right after the conjugated verb, not before it.
Swedish V2 rule: the verb is always second in main clauses.
"Ska" implies intention, "kommer att" implies prediction.
When an adverb starts the sentence, subject and verb swap: "Idag åker jag" = Today I go.
In subordinate clauses they stay together: "...att jag ringer upp dig".
Modal verbs: "kan" (can), "ska" (shall), "vill" (want), "måste" (must), "bör" (should).
Swedish future uses "ska" (will/shall) or "kommer att" (going to).
'Sig' is the reflexive for han/hon/de: 'Han tvättar sig' (He washes himself).
In subordinate clauses, "inte" goes before the verb.
Sentence adverbs never appear between the subject and verb in Swedish main clauses — they always follow the conjugated verb.
Modals are followed by the infinitive without "att": "Jag kan simma" = I can swim.
"Inte" goes after the verb in main clauses: "Jag förstår inte" = I don't understand.
Frequency adverbs like 'ofta' and 'sällan' sit after the verb in main clauses but before it in subordinate clauses.
Common-gender (en) nouns add '-en' for definite singular: 'en bok' → 'boken'. Neuter (ett) nouns add '-et': 'ett barn' → 'barnet'.
When you see 'alltid', 'aldrig', or 'ofta' in a Swedish sentence, check if it's a main or subordinate clause to know where to place it.
Swedish double-marks definiteness when using adjectives: 'den stora boken' needs both 'den' and the '-en' suffix.
Plural definite forms depend on the declension group: '-na' for most en-words, '-en' or '-a' for ett-words in plural.
The adverb position flips between main and subordinate clauses: 'Jag dricker aldrig...' vs. 'att jag aldrig dricker...'
Remember: 'inte' after the verb in main clauses ('Han köper inte'), but before in subclauses ('att han inte köper').
Swedish subordinate clauses: 'inte' and other adverbs go BEFORE the verb, not after like in main clauses.
The definite suffix attaches directly to the noun — no separate article needed unless an adjective comes between.
Time and manner adverbs have more flexibility, but negation ('inte') and frequency adverbs strictly follow verb-position rules.
Swedish adverb placement is tied to clause type — after the verb in main clauses, before it in subclauses starting with att/som/när.
Swedish definite nouns look different from English 'the': the article is fused onto the end, making Swedish nouns longer in definite form.
The BIFF rule (Bisats Inte Före Finita verbet) helps remember: in subclauses, 'inte' comes before the finite verb.
Geographical names and proper nouns in Swedish don't take definite suffixes, but days and meals often do: 'frukosten' (the breakfast).
Swedish time adverbs: always after the verb in main clauses, before the verb in subordinate clauses.
Possessives replace the definite suffix: 'min bok' (my book) not 'min boken' — you don't double-mark possession and definiteness.
Place 'inte' (not) directly after the verb in main clauses: 'Jag äter inte' — but in subclauses it moves before the verb.
Abstract and uncountable nouns also take definite suffixes in Swedish: 'maten' (the food), 'vädret' (the weather).
When you see a noun ending in '-en', '-et', '-na', or '-erna', it's likely carrying a definite suffix rather than being a new word.
Swedish marks definiteness with a suffix on the noun itself: 'hund' → 'hunden' (the dog), 'hus' → 'huset' (the house).

welsh.tip: "Mae'r" contracts "Mae" + "y/yr" (the): used before definite nouns.
"Mae" is the present tense third-person form of "bod" (to be) — the cornerstone of Welsh sentences.
The particle "yn" (shortened to 'n after vowels) links "bod" to adjectives or verb-nouns.
"Roedd" is the imperfect (was/were) form of "bod" — used for past states and ongoing past actions.
"Bydd" is the future form of "bod" — "Bydda i'n" = I will be.
"Wedi" + verb-noun = have done — Welsh perfect tense: "Dw i wedi bwyta" = I have eaten.
"Dw i'n" is the spoken form of "Rydw i'n" (I am...) — the most common sentence pattern in Welsh.
"Ei" (his/her) triggers different mutations: "ei" (his) = soft mutation, "ei" (her) = aspirate mutation.
"Rhaid" (must/necessity) — Welsh expresses obligation as "necessity is to me": "Rhaid i fi".
Welsh has formal (chi) and informal (ti) forms, like French tu/vous.
Welsh job titles often end in "-wr" (masc) or "-wraig" (fem): athro/athrawes.
"Er bod..." = "although..." — takes a clause with "bod".
Welsh has no word for "have" — you say "Mae gen i" (there is with me).
Some imperatives are irregular: "cer/dos" (go!), "tyrd/dere" (come!).
"Y Gymraeg" (the Welsh language) — note the soft mutation after "y" feminine.
Time uses "o'r gloch" (of the bell) like English "o'clock".
After masculine "ei" (his): "ei gar" (his car). After feminine "ei": aspirate mutation.
"I'r" is a contraction of "i" (to) + "y/yr" (the): "i'r dde" = to the right.
Adjectives soften after feminine nouns: "merch dal" ← "tal", "cath ddu" ← "du".
Feminine adjectives take soft mutation: "merch dal" (tall girl) from "tal".
Aspirate mutation after feminine "ei" (her): car→ei char, pen→ei phen, tad→ei thad.
The imperfect describes ongoing states and actions in the past, like "was doing".
"Yn" as predicative particle triggers soft mutation: "Mae'n dda" ← "da".
"Ga i...?" (May I?) is from "cael" (to get/have) — triggers soft mutation.
Welsh has two genders: masculine and feminine. "Y" is used for "the" before both.
"Faswn i ddim yn..." = "I wouldn't..." — negative conditional.
Imperfect is used for background actions: "Roeddwn i'n cerdded pan welodd e fi."
"Dylwn i" (I should) — "dylwn" is the conditional of "dylu" (to owe/ought).
"Fydda i ddim..." = "I won't be..." — negative future.
Welsh uses fronting for emphasis: "Coffi dw i eisiau" = It's COFFEE I want.
"Fi sy'n..." = "It's me who..." — cleft structure for emphasis.
Welsh imperative 2sg: use the verb stem: "agor!" (open!), "cau!" (close!).
"Chi" is the polite/formal form; "ti" is informal — like French "vous/tu".
Welsh comparatives: add "-ach" to adjective: tal→talach, cyflym→cyflymach.
"Bydda i'n..." = "I will be doing..." — periphrastic future.
"A" is the relative pronoun that triggers soft mutation: "Y ferch a welodd" = The girl who saw.
